_link.title: I can outline how reactions proceed differently in open and closed systems

toLevel2.stem: In an open system, what happens to gaseous products?
distractors: They remain inside the vessel
They convert back to reactants
They are absorbed by the liquid

toLevel2.stem: In a closed system, what happens to all reactants and products?
toLevel2.answer: They remain within the reaction vessel
distractors: They escape into the surroundings
They are lost to the atmosphere
They evaporate out of the container

toLevel2.stem: What type of system allows gases to escape to the surroundings?
distractors: A closed system
An isolated system
A sealed system

toLevel2.stem: When magnesium reacts with HCl in an open flask, the hydrogen gas produced:
distractors: stays inside the flask
dissolves in the acid
reacts with the magnesium

toLevel2.stem: When magnesium reacts with HCl in a sealed flask, the hydrogen gas produced:
distractors: escapes into the air
is destroyed by the reaction
converts back into HCl

toLevel2.stem: In an open system, gaseous products escape and cannot re-react with the remaining reactants.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: In a closed system, gaseous products can escape to the surroundings.
distractors: True

toLevel2.stem: In an open system, gaseous products {{blank:1}} to the surroundings, while in a closed system they {{blank:2}} inside the vessel.
distractors: remain
escape

toLevel2.stem: Hydrogen gas released from Mg + HCl in an open flask escapes into the {{blank:1}}, but in a sealed flask it {{blank:2}} inside.
distractors: liquid
dissolves
acid

toLevel3.stem: Why does the system type affect the extent of a reaction?
toLevel3.answer: In a closed system, product build-up can influence the reaction; in an open system, escaping gases are lost permanently
distractors: The system type changes the activation energy of the reaction
The system type determines the kinetic energy of the particles
The system type has no effect on any aspect of the reaction

toLevel3.stem: Why can escaped gases in an open system not re-react?
toLevel3.answer: They disperse into the surroundings and are no longer in contact with the other reactants
distractors: They lose all kinetic energy and become unable to collide
They change into a different substance once they leave the flask
They are absorbed by the atmosphere and destroyed permanently

toLevel3.stem: Why might a reaction go to completion more readily in an open system than in a closed system?
toLevel3.answer: Gaseous products escape and cannot participate in any reverse reaction
distractors: Open systems have lower activation energies than closed systems
Closed systems prevent any reactions from occurring at all
Open systems increase the kinetic energy of reactant particles

toLevel3.stem: In a closed system, what effect does the accumulation of gaseous products have?
toLevel3.answer: The products can potentially participate in a reverse reaction
distractors: The products increase the temperature of the reaction mixture
The products lower the activation energy of the forward reaction
The products are immediately destroyed by the excess reactants

toLevel3.stem: How does the system type affect the monitoring of reaction rate?
toLevel3.answer: In an open system, mass loss can be measured as gas escapes; in a closed system, gas must be collected internally
distractors: Rate can only be measured in a closed system, never in an open system
Rate can only be measured in an open system, never in a closed system
The system type has no effect on how rate can be measured

toLevel3.stem: Why is it important to specify whether a reaction occurs in an open or closed system?
toLevel3.answer: It affects the interpretation of experimental data and whether products can accumulate
distractors: It is only relevant for reactions that do not produce any gas at all
It only matters for industrial reactions, not laboratory experiments
It has no importance because all reactions behave identically in both systems

toLevel3.stem: A reaction in an open system may go to completion more readily because gaseous products escape and cannot participate in a reverse reaction.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: In a closed system, gaseous products can {{blank:1}} and potentially participate in a {{blank:2}} reaction.
distractors: escape
forward
dissolve
faster

toLevel3.stem: An open system allows gases to {{blank:1}}, which means they are permanently {{blank:2}} from the reaction.
distractors: accumulate
added
dissolve
absorbed

toLevel3.stem: The system type affects whether product {{blank:1}} builds up, which influences the rate and {{blank:2}} of the reaction.
distractors: mass
temperature
energy
colour

toLevel4.stem: A student reacts zinc with sulfuric acid in an open beaker. Hydrogen gas is produced. Why will this reaction go to completion?
toLevel4.answer: The hydrogen gas escapes and cannot reverse the reaction
distractors: The beaker prevents any gas from being produced during the reaction
Open beakers always have lower activation energies than sealed flasks
Zinc cannot react in a closed system under any conditions

toLevel4.stem: A chemist carries out the same reaction in both an open flask and a sealed flask. In which system would they expect to measure mass loss?
toLevel4.answer: The open flask, where gas escapes and reduces the total mass
distractors: The sealed flask, where gas accumulates and adds mass
Both systems would show identical mass loss patterns
Neither system would show any change in mass at all

toLevel4.stem: A student places a conical flask on a balance and adds acid to marble chips. They leave the flask open. The balance reading decreases over time. Why?
toLevel4.answer: CO₂ gas is produced and escapes from the open flask
distractors: The marble chips are evaporating into the atmosphere
The acid is leaking out of the bottom of the flask
The balance is losing accuracy as time passes

toLevel4.stem: A student performs the same gas-producing reaction in an open flask and a sealed flask. If they measure the total mass of each system at the end, what will they find?
toLevel4.answer: The open flask has lost mass; the sealed flask has the same mass as at the start
distractors: Both flasks have lost the same amount of mass
The sealed flask has lost more mass than the open flask
Neither flask has changed in mass at all

toLevel4.stem: A student wants to collect all the gas produced in a reaction for analysis. Should they use an open or closed system?
toLevel4.answer: A closed system, so no gas escapes and all products are retained
distractors: An open system, so the gas can be collected as it escapes
Either system would work because gas collection does not depend on the system type
An open system, because closed systems prevent gas from forming

toLevel4.stem: A reaction produces ammonia gas (NH₃). In an open system, the ammonia escapes. In a closed system, the ammonia builds up. How might this difference affect the reaction?
toLevel4.answer: In the closed system, the ammonia build-up could slow the forward reaction or enable a reverse reaction
distractors: The ammonia build-up in the closed system would increase the forward reaction rate
The open system would have a slower forward reaction because ammonia provides energy
There would be no difference because ammonia has no effect on the reaction

toLevel4.stem: A student is told that conservation of mass applies to chemical reactions. They weigh an open flask before and after a gas-producing reaction and find the mass has decreased. Does this violate conservation of mass?
toLevel4.answer: No — mass is conserved overall; the gas has simply escaped the system
distractors: Yes — mass should always stay the same inside the flask
No — mass is never conserved in chemical reactions
Yes — gas production always violates conservation of mass

toLevel4.stem: In an open flask, CO₂ escapes and the balance reading {{blank:1}}, while in a sealed flask the mass remains {{blank:2}}.
distractors: increases
variable
fluctuates
zero

toLevel4.stem: A student who wants to collect all the gas from a reaction should use a {{blank:1}} system so that no gas {{blank:2}}.
distractors: open
accumulates

toLevel4.stem: Conservation of mass is not violated in an open system — the gas has simply {{blank:1}} the system, taking its {{blank:2}} with it.
distractors: entered

toLevel5.stem: A reversible reaction is carried out in both an open and a closed system. In the open system, the gaseous product escapes. How does this affect the final yield of products compared to the closed system?
toLevel5.answer: The open system gives a higher yield because the forward reaction is driven to completion
distractors: The closed system gives a higher yield because products are retained
Both systems give the same yield regardless of whether gas escapes
The open system gives a lower yield because escaping gas removes energy

toLevel5.stem: A student claims: 'Closed systems are always better for chemical reactions because no matter is lost.' Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Not always — in some reactions, removing a gaseous product (open system) is desirable to drive the reaction to completion
distractors: Correct — closed systems are always superior for every type of reaction
Incorrect — open systems are always better because they prevent pressure build-up
Correct — losing matter always reduces the efficiency of a reaction

toLevel5.stem: In a closed system, a gas-producing reaction reaches a state where the forward and reverse rates are equal. Why can this state not be achieved in an open system?
toLevel5.answer: The gaseous product escapes and cannot participate in the reverse reaction
distractors: Open systems have higher temperatures that prevent equilibrium from forming
Closed systems do not allow any forward reactions to occur at all
The activation energy is different in open and closed systems

toLevel5.stem: A peer states: 'The system type only matters for reactions that produce gases.' Is this a complete assessment?
toLevel5.answer: Mostly correct at VCE level, but volatile liquids can also escape from open systems
distractors: Completely correct — system type is irrelevant for reactions without gas production
Completely incorrect — system type matters for all reactions equally
Mostly incorrect — system type only matters for solid-state reactions

toLevel5.stem: A student measures the rate of a gas-producing reaction in both an open and closed system at the same temperature and concentration. Would the initial rates differ?
toLevel5.answer: The initial rates should be very similar because product build-up has not yet occurred
distractors: The open system would have a much higher initial rate than the closed system
The closed system would have a much higher initial rate than the open system
The initial rates cannot be compared between open and closed systems

toLevel5.stem: In an industrial process, a chemist deliberately removes a gaseous product as it forms. What is the purpose of this strategy?
toLevel5.answer: To drive the forward reaction to completion by preventing the reverse reaction
distractors: To slow down the reaction by removing products from the system
To increase the activation energy and make the reaction more controlled
To decrease the temperature of the reaction mixture

toLevel5.stem: A student compares mass-time graphs for the same reaction in an open and sealed flask. The open flask shows mass decreasing; the sealed flask shows mass constant. Both run for the same duration. What can be concluded about the total amount of reaction?
toLevel5.answer: The same amount of reaction may occur, but only the open system shows detectable mass change
distractors: The open system has more reaction because it shows a mass change
The sealed system has no reaction because the mass does not change
Mass change always indicates more reaction than constant mass

toLevel5.stem: A student argues: 'Since mass is conserved, there is no point measuring mass loss in an open system.' Why is this argument flawed?
toLevel5.answer: Mass loss from the flask accurately tracks the amount of gas produced, even though total mass is conserved overall
distractors: The argument is correct — mass loss measurements are meaningless in open systems
Mass is not conserved in open systems, so the measurement is always invalid
Mass loss only works in closed systems where gas accumulates inside

distractors: equilibrium
